content.text: Calculate how the purchasing power of the U.S. dollar has changed from 1913 to 2025112 Years of Data (1913-2025)Official BLS CPI-U DataReal-Time CalculationsDebt-Inflation AnalysisThe current US inflation rate is 2.9% as of April 2026, based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Since 1913, the dollar has lost over 97% of its purchasing power. The baseline cost has permanently shifted upward.Key insight: "Disinflation" (prices rising slower) is not the same as "deflation" (prices actually falling). Most essentials are in disinflation territory—still getting more expensive, just at a slower pace.The "Silent Pay Cut": 25.6% Loss Since 2020If your salary hasn't increased by at least 26% since January 2020, you've effectively taken a pay cut.2020 Salary$100,000Nominal valueToday's Buying Power$79,617In 2020 dollars"Break Even" Salary$125,642Needed to match 2020Year-by-Year Erosion of $100kWhere Did the Money Go? Over 5 years, this gap means your 'cost of living' raise pushes you deeper into higher tax brackets.2020 Tax ReturnGross Salary$100,000Standard Deduction-$12,400Federal Tax$15,103Effective Rate15.1%In 24% Bracket$2,0752025 Tax Return (with "break-even" salary)Gross Salary$125,600Standard Deduction-$15,750Federal Tax$19,211Effective Rate15.3%In 24% Bracket$6,500The Result: Even though you were only given a raise to match inflation, the government took a larger slice. Your tax bill grew 27.2% while income only grew 25.6%.The Bottom LineIf you have not received a raise of at least 26% over the last 5 years, you are technically poorer today than you were before the pandemic. And due to bracket creep, you actually need ~$126,500 to truly break even after taxes.Reverse Calculator: What Was It Worth?To have the same buying power as $100 today, how much would you have needed in the past?Today's Amount ($)In What Year?$100 today had the same purchasing power as $12.37 in 1970. That's a 709% decrease in buying power.How Inflation Affects the $38.91T National DebtInflation doesn't just affect your wallet—it fundamentally changes how we understand the national debt.The 1913 National Debt in Today's DollarsWhen the Federal Reserve was created in 1913, the national debt was ~$3 billion. Adjusted for inflation, that's equivalent to ~$92.40B today.Today's Debt in 1913 DollarsIf we measured today's debt in 1913 purchasing power, it would be ~$1.23T. Real debt growth far exceeds inflation.Debt Erosion (Annual Benefit)~1.10T/yearInflation erodes the real value of existing debt, effectively reducing what the government owes in purchasing power terms.Higher Interest Costs (Risk)~39.49B/yearHigher inflation leads to higher interest rates, increasing the cost of servicing existing debt and new borrowing.The Double-Edged SwordGovernments can "inflate away" debt by letting inflation reduce its real value. However, this comes at a cost: it erodes savings, raises interest rates, and disproportionately hurts those on fixed incomes. The Federal Reserve's 2% target attempts to balance economic growth with debt sustainability—but with debt at 139% of GDP, the margin for error is shrinking.Annual Inflation Rates (2015-2025)201620172018201920202021202220232024202520260%2%4%6%8%What $1 From the Past is Worth Today$1 in 1913$31.69in 2024 dollars$1 in 1950$13.02in 2024 dollars$1 in 1970$8.09in 2024 dollars$1 in 1980$3.81in 2024 dollars$1 in 1990$2.40in 2024 dollars$1 in 2000$1.82in 2024 dollars$1 in 2010$1.44in 2024 dollars$1 in 2015$1.32in 2024 dollars$1 in 2020$1.21in 2024 dollars$1 in 2022$1.07in 2024 dollars$1 in 1913 (when the Federal Reserve was created) has the same purchasing power as $31.69 today— a 3069% decrease in the dollar's value.Price Changes: 2000 vs 20242000: $21,7502024: $48,5002000: $119,6002024: $420,000CPI Trend (Last 2 Years)2023-062024-012024-032024-052024-072024-092024-112025-012025-032025-052025-072025-092026-01296304312320328Related Tools & DataFrequently Asked QuestionsHow does the inflation calculator work?Our inflation calculator uses the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It compares the CPI values between your selected years to calculate how much money you would need in one year to have the same purchasing power as in another year.What is the CPI?The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the average change in prices paid by urban consumers for a basket of goods and services over time. The base period is 1982-84 = 100. A CPI of 314 means prices are 214% higher than they were in the base period.Why does inflation matter for the national debt?Inflation affects the national debt in two ways: (1) it erodes the real value of existing debt, which benefits the government, and (2) it typically leads to higher interest rates, which increases the cost of servicing the debt. Our calculator helps you understand these dynamics.How accurate is this inflation calculator?Our calculator uses official BLS CPI-U (Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers) annual averages from 1913 to present. This is the same data used by government agencies and economists for inflation adjustments.How does the retirement inflation calculator work?The retirement calculator projects how inflation will erode your savings' purchasing power over time. It uses compound inflation to show what your current savings will be worth in "today's dollars" at retirement, helping you understand the real gap between what you've saved and what you'll need.Your Personal Inflation ScoreThe 2.9% headline rate is an average. Your actual inflation depends on what you spend money on.Data SourcesCPI data from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), 1913-present. Price comparisons from BLS average price data. National debt data from U.S. Treasury. Live data from FRED API. Last updated: January 2026.
